title: Chronic dry cough post-MI: review meds (ACE inhibitor cough)
vignette: A 56-year-old woman presents to your office with chronic cough. She says that the cough is dry and affects quality of her life significantly. She denies chest pain, hemoptysis, and shortness of breath. Her past medical history is significant for long-standing hypertension, diabetes and myocardial infarction experienced two months ago. She does not smoke or consume alcohol. Her blood pressure is 130/70 mmHg and heart rate is 70/min. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient?

clues.note: A DRY, nonproductive, persistent cough is the classic character of ACE inhibitor-induced cough.

clues.text: long-standing hypertension, diabetes and myocardial infarction experienced two months ago
clues.note: This profile (hypertension, diabetes, recent MI) makes ACE inhibitor therapy highly likely - a common cause of a new dry cough.

clues.text: does not smoke or consume alcohol
clues.note: No smoking lowers the likelihood of COPD/malignancy, further pointing to a drug-induced cough.

whatMatters: A new DRY, persistent cough in a patient very likely on an ACE INHIBITOR (hypertension + diabetes + post-MI) is most likely ACE inhibitor-induced cough. The best next step is to REVIEW the CURRENT MEDICATIONS to identify (and consider stopping) the ACE inhibitor. Answer C.
strategy: Recognize the classic ACE inhibitor cough and confirm the culprit by reviewing the medication list before pursuing an expensive/invasive workup. Reject family history (cough isn't hereditary here), allergy history (no atopic features), diet/exercise (irrelevant to cough), and chest x-ray (no red flags - no hemoptysis, weight loss, or smoking - so imaging isn't the FIRST step).

options.text: Careful review of past allergic episodes
Careful review of diet and physical activity

eliminations.label: Family history - cough isn't the clue (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: screening the family history for hereditary disease. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: a dry cough in a likely ACE-inhibitor user points to a medication effect; family history won't identify the cause here. ✅ Correct if: suspecting a hereditary condition (e.g., cancer risk assessment).

eliminations.label: Past allergic episodes - no atopic features
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: reviewing allergies (e.g., postnasal drip from allergic rhinitis). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: she has no allergic symptoms (itchy/watery eyes, rhinorrhea), and the presentation fits a drug cough. ✅ Correct if: allergic rhinitis/upper airway cough syndrome features.

eliminations.label: Diet and physical activity - unrelated to cough
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: reviewing lifestyle factors. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: diet/exercise do not cause a chronic dry cough and won't identify the ACE inhibitor. ✅ Correct if: cardiovascular risk-factor counseling, not cough workup.

eliminations.label: Chest x-ray - not the first step without red flags
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: imaging to look for pneumonia, malignancy, or other lung disease. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: with no hemoptysis, weight loss, or smoking history and a likely drug cause, reviewing medications comes first (imaging if cough persists after stopping the ACE inhibitor). ✅ Correct if: red-flag features (hemoptysis, weight loss, abnormal exam) suggesting serious lung disease.

reasoning: New chronic DRY cough in a patient very likely on an ACE inhibitor (hypertension, diabetes, post-MI)
ACE inhibitor cough is a common, well-known adverse effect (bradykinin/substance P accumulation)
Best next step is to review the medication list to identify the ACE inhibitor before further workup
-> careful review of current medications; answer C
mechanism: A persistent DRY, nonproductive cough is one of the most recognized adverse effects of ACE INHIBITOR therapy - and this patient's profile (long-standing hypertension, diabetes, and a recent myocardial infarction) makes an ACE inhibitor highly likely. Angiotensin-converting enzyme is nonspecific and also degrades BRADYKININ and substance P; ACE inhibition allows these mediators to ACCUMULATE, causing airway inflammation and cough (it can also predispose to angioedema). The cough can appear anytime from days to months after starting the drug and resolves after discontinuation. Because angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) do NOT affect bradykinin metabolism, switching to an ARB typically relieves the cough. Therefore, the most appropriate FIRST step is a careful review of the current medication list to identify the ACE inhibitor (then discontinue/substitute), reserving imaging for red-flag features or persistence after stopping the drug. Family history, allergy history, and diet/exercise reviews would not identify this drug-induced cough.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Pharm > ACE inhibitors: dry cough (bradykinin/substance P accumulation) and angioedema; ARBs don't cause cough (no bradykinin effect).

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Likely ACE-inhibitor user + new dry cough -> review medications first (identify the culprit).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on ACE inhibitor, bradykinin, ARB vs ACE inhibitor, or 'best next step'? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Family/allergy history and diet won't find the drug cough; chest x-ray isn't first without red flags.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: ACE inhibitor cough = bradykinin/substance P buildup; review meds, switch to ARB; imaging only if red flags/persists.
